## June 23, 1956

On the day you were born, Gamal Abdel Nasser was confirmed as President of Egypt in a national referendum — winning, as authoritarian referendums tend to go, with nearly unanimous approval. It would have seemed a regional story, the consolidation of power by a charismatic military officer in a country still finding its post-colonial footing. Thirty-three days later, Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal, and the world discovered exactly what kind of force it had ratified on your birthday.

**The Suez Crisis is one of the most consequential events of the postwar order**, and you were an infant at its exact center of gravity. Britain and France, accustomed to treating the Canal as theirs by right of imperial custom, coordinated a secret invasion with Israel in October 1956. Egyptian forces were defeated militarily. It did not matter. President Eisenhower — furious at being kept out of the plan — threatened economic consequences severe enough that Britain and France were forced to withdraw in humiliation. The message was unmistakable: the age of European imperial power was over. The United States would be the Western hegemon. Anti-colonial nationalism, which Nasser personified, had found a superpower patron in the USSR and an unlikely disciplinarian in the US. The world order you have lived your entire life under was shaped, in significant part, by what happened in those months surrounding your birth.

**Six days after you were born**, on June 29, 1956, President Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act into law — authorizing 41,000 miles of interstate highways, the largest public works project in American history. This did not feel like a birth announcement, but it was: of the suburban nation, the car culture, the American geography of strip malls and drive-throughs and commuter distances that defines the physical landscape you grew up in. The highway system restructured where Americans lived, how they shopped, which downtowns thrived and which hollowed out. It is still the armature of the country.

**The civil rights movement was entering one of its decisive passages.** The Montgomery Bus Boycott — triggered by Rosa Parks's refusal to give up her seat in December 1955 — was in its seventh month when you were born. The Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama were sustaining a community-wide economic protest against bus segregation through carpools and walking and mutual support, under constant harassment and legal pressure. The boycott would end in December 1956, when the Supreme Court's ruling took effect and Montgomery's buses were desegregated. You were born during the months between the spark and the victory — during the proof that disciplined collective action could win.

**The communist world was quietly fracturing.** Four months before your birth, in February 1956, Nikita Khrushchev had delivered his "Secret Speech" to the Soviet Communist Party congress — a devastating denunciation of Stalin's crimes, his cult of personality, his purges and show trials. The speech was not meant to leave the room. It leaked. The effect on communist parties worldwide was seismic: the ideology that millions had built their lives around was being repudiated from within by its own leadership. By October 1956, Hungary rose in revolution, and Soviet tanks crushed it. The Cold War you grew up in was not a stable equilibrium; it was a sustained internal argument about what each side actually stood for.

**And 1956 was the year rock and roll became inescapable.** "Heartbreak Hotel" had hit number one in April. By the time you were born, Elvis Presley was not yet a cultural institution — he was a scandal, an argument at dinner tables, something parents worried about and teenagers felt had been made specifically for them. He appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show in September, filmed from the waist up by nervous network executives. The popular culture you were born into was in the middle of being permanently reorganized by a sound that had come out of Black American music and was now going everywhere.

---

**What seventy years looks like:**

You were six during the Cuban Missile Crisis — too young to understand the briefings, old enough to practice duck-and-cover drills and notice the adults around you in a state of controlled fear. You were twelve during 1968, which remains among the most violent, fractured years in modern American history: King killed in April, Kennedy killed in June, the Democratic convention in August, cities burning. You were thirteen when humans walked on the Moon.

Vietnam defined your young adulthood in a specific way: you were born too late to fight in it, but old enough to watch it end in April 1975, when you were eighteen — old enough to understand what a war's collapse looked like on television. Watergate arrived when you were seventeen. The Iranian Revolution when you were twenty-two. The Berlin Wall fell when you were thirty-three. September 11 when you were forty-five. COVID when you were sixty-three.

You turned seventy this past June. You entered a world without jet air travel as a mass phenomenon, without television in most homes, without antibiotics having existed for more than a decade — and you have lived into a world of pocket computers, genomic medicine, and artificial intelligence that can converse, generate, and reason.

---

You were born on the day the architect of the Suez Crisis was formally elevated to power, at the precise moment when the imperial geography of the twentieth century was about to be redrawn. It is a birth date with a particular quality: the world it came into was recognizably the old world, and the world it produced, in the months that immediately followed, was recognizably the new one.
